title: Why Every Python Project Needs Its Own Environment
excerpt: Install third-party packages with pip and stop projects from breaking each other by giving each one its own virtual environment.

headings.text: Activate It and Install Into It

html:
Python's real power comes from the huge collection of packages that other people have written: tools for web requests, data analysis, charts, machine learning and thousands of other jobs. You install them with a tool called pip. Installing is easy. The trouble starts when you have more than one project.

A virtual environment is a private folder holding its own copy of Python's tools and its own installed packages, so each project can have exactly the versions it needs. This lesson explains the problem it solves, creates a real environment, and shows the commands you will use every day.

The Problem: Projects That Disagree

Imagine project A was written against version 1 of a package, and project B needs version 2, which behaves differently. If you install packages into your computer's one shared Python, installing version 2 for project B can silently break project A. A shared pile of packages becomes a puzzle nobody can untangle. How do you give each project its own set?

pip Installs Packages

pip is Python's package installer. It downloads packages (bundles of modules that other people have published) from the Python Package Index, usually called PyPI, and puts them where Python can import them. You run it from the terminal (the text window where you type commands), not inside a Python program:

pip install requests
pip list
pip uninstall requests

Here install downloads a package, list shows what is installed, and uninstall removes one. Where do the packages end up? Python has a special folder for them, called site-packages. This small check prints True because the folder Python uses for installed packages really is named that:

import sysconfig

folder = sysconfig.get_paths()["purelib"]
print(folder.endswith("site-packages"))
True

Create a Virtual Environment

The built-in venv module creates an environment. From the terminal the command is python -m venv .venv, which makes a folder called .venv in your project. To show exactly what it builds, the example below runs that same terminal command from inside Python (you do not need to understand the Python used to launch it; focus on the output) and lists the result:

import os
import subprocess
import sys

subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "venv", "demo_env"], check=True)
print(sorted(os.listdir("demo_env")))
['.gitignore', 'bin', 'include', 'lib', 'pyvenv.cfg']

This listing is from macOS or Linux with a recent Python. The bin folder holds a private copy of the python and pip programs, lib is where this environment's own packages will go, and pyvenv.cfg is a small settings file. The .gitignore file is added by recent Python versions so that Git, a tool that tracks changes to your files, ignores the folder automatically, and include holds files used when building packages, which you can ignore. On Windows the folders are named Scripts and Lib, and details can vary slightly between Python versions.

Prove It Is Separate

Running the environment's own Python and asking where it lives confirms that it is a separate world from your main Python (on Windows the program is demo_env\Scripts\python):

result = subprocess.run(
    ["demo_env/bin/python", "-c", "import sys; print(sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix)"],
    capture_output=True,
    text=True,
)
print(result.stdout.strip())
True

The answer True means this Python knows it is running inside a virtual environment: its own location (the prefix) differs from the base Python it was created from.

Activate It and Install Into It

Typing the full path to the environment's Python every time would be tedious, so you activate the environment. Activation adjusts your terminal so that python and pip mean the environment's own copies:

# macOS and Linux
source .venv/bin/activate

# Windows
.venv\Scripts\activate

pip install requests

deactivate

While the environment is active, your terminal prompt usually starts with (.venv), and pip install puts packages into that environment only. Does that fix project A and project B? Yes: give each project its own .venv and each one keeps its own versions. When you are done, deactivate returns you to your normal terminal.

Share Your Package List

How does a teammate (or you, on another computer) recreate the same environment? You record the installed packages in a text file, conventionally named requirements.txt, and install from it:

pip freeze > requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements.txt

The first command writes every installed package, with its exact version, into the file (> saves a command's output into a file). The second installs all of them in a fresh environment (-r means "read the list from this file"). The environment folder itself is large and easy to rebuild, so it is normally kept out of version control (a system that tracks changes to your files), and only requirements.txt is shared.

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonPipVirtualEnvironments.ipynb.

Summary

  • pip installs packages from PyPI; run it in the terminal with pip install name.
  • Packages installed into one shared Python can clash between projects.
  • python -m venv .venv creates a private environment with its own Python and package folder.
  • Activate it (source .venv/bin/activate on macOS and Linux, .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows) so python and pip use it.
  • pip freeze > requirements.txt records your packages; pip install -r requirements.txt recreates them.
  • Create one environment per project, and share requirements.txt, not the environment folder.
